why: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the mid-200s, told his congregation, when plague struck, that caring only for their own was nothing great, before he was beheaded outside the city in 258. A century and a half later, at Hippo, Augustine preached in church and in homes, and listeners, the rival church's people too, brought shorthand writers to take down what he said.
sourcing: Rich (Cyprian's letters, Augustine's sermons to his own flock)
floorNote: Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed states.
relationsSummary: The churches led by Cyprian at Carthage and Augustine at Hippo. From the 310s a rival Donatist church stood in the same towns.
teaser: Roman North Africa, the 250s to 430 CE — the parish before the word existed: bishops gathering their people through plague, judging their quarrels, and deciding what to do about the people who had failed.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius until his death in 430, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and cataloged his works
legacy: The North African church itself did not survive. The Vandals took the province in the 430s. The Arab conquest came in the seventh century. After it, Latin Christianity there slowly died out. What it left behind is the working vocabulary of Western church life. Cyprian's letters laid the ground for how the West thinks about the bishop's office and the unity of the church. Later, the Donatists quoted them in their own defense. Augustine's sermons shaped Christian preaching for well over a thousand years. These congregations also worked out the catechumenate, the training of new believers before baptism. They worked out the practice of penance too. Both became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline. In Geneva, Calvin wrote that he could fill a whole book with Augustine's words on God's choice of the saved. Latin Christianity's basic ideas about what a local church is took shape largely in these two African towns. Both churches claimed Cyprian: when the Donatists brought his authority forward for baptizing again, Augustine answered that they should keep Cyprian's example of unity instead. On Cyprian's feast Augustine preached that where a savage crowd had once gathered to shed his blood, a crowd now gathered to honor him, at an altar called Cyprian's table because he was offered there. Possidius copied Augustine's letter on clergy staying with their people into his Life, as very useful, even necessary, for priests. After Augustine's death, Hippo, abandoned by its people, was burned by the enemy. A century later, Procopius says, the people of Carthage revered Cyprian above all saints and kept a festival called the Cypriana at his church by the sea, which the Vandals had taken from the Christians. More than a century after Augustine, Facundus, a bishop of Byzantine Africa, still called Cyprian bishop of Carthage and martyr, and Augustine the most wise and most famous teacher of the churches of Christ.

documentedStories.title: Cyprian’s Flight and the Sneer from Rome
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: When the persecution comes, the bishop of Carthage withdraws. The clergy of Rome, whose own bishop has just been killed, write to ask why.
documentedStories.text: Decius’ order that everyone sacrifice reached Carthage early in 250, and the crowd in the amphitheater was already shouting for Cyprian by name. He left the city. The Roman clergy, whose bishop Fabian had just been executed, wrote to the Carthaginian clergy a letter that Cyprian later had to answer. It opened by noting that they had heard ‘the blessed father Cyprian has for a certain reason withdrawn’, and went on to quote the Gospel: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, but ‘the hireling, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth.’ It was not subtle. Cyprian’s reply, and the stream of letters he sent from hiding, make his case: his presence would provoke worse violence against the congregation; he had continued to govern the church by correspondence; he had ordered the clergy to keep visiting the imprisoned confessors, and to do it in shifts and in ordinary dress so as not to draw attention. ‘Nothing on my own private opinion,’ he wrote of the readmission of the lapsed, promising to decide with the clergy and people when he could return. He did return, faced down a schism over exactly this question, and eight years later stood trial without flinching. But the charge of cowardice followed him, and his own biographer Pontius spends paragraphs answering it. The record keeps both the flight and the reasons.
documentedStories.caveat: All the letters are contemporary and Cyprian preserved even the hostile one; but the collection was assembled by his own church, and his side of the argument is far better represented than the Roman clergy’s.

documentedStories.title: The Night Watch Outside the Officer’s House
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Carthage learns that its bishop has been brought in, and the congregation spends the night in the street.
documentedStories.text: Under Valerian’s second edict, bishops were to be executed. Cyprian was arrested at his garden estate and taken to the proconsul’s residence, then, because the hearing was put off to the next day, held overnight at the house of an officer of the guard. Pontius, his deacon, was there. He says a rumor ran through the city ‘that now Thascius was brought forward’, and that everyone came — ‘to us glorious from the devotion of faith, and to be mourned over even by the Gentiles.’ The custody was gentle; the friends were allowed in. And ‘the whole people, in anxiety that nothing should be done throughout the night without their knowledge, kept watch before the officer’s door.’ Pontius’ comment is that God granted that ‘God’s people should watch on the passion of the priest’. The next morning the proconsul Galerius Maximus asked Cyprian to confirm his name and to perform the rites; the official record of the exchange, the Acta, gives his refusal in a handful of words and the sentence: to be executed by the sword. Cyprian said ‘Thanks be to God’, and the crowd, by Pontius’ account, cried out to be killed with him. He was beheaded in a field outside the city, having ordered that the executioner be paid twenty-five gold pieces. The vigil is the detail to keep: a congregation that had watched him flee eight years earlier now stood all night outside a door.
documentedStories.caveat: Pontius was an eyewitness writing within a year or two, but as a devoted biographer; the trial dialogue rests on the Acta Proconsularia, a separate court-style record whose text has been lightly edited in transmission.

documentedStories.title: The Psalms on the Wall of Augustine’s Room
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: With the Vandals outside Hippo, an old bishop asks for the penitential psalms to be written out and hung where he can see them.
documentedStories.text: Possidius, bishop of Calama, had known Augustine for nearly forty years and was in Hippo Regius when the Vandal army closed round it in the summer of 430. His Life of Augustine, written within a few years, describes the end. Refugee bishops and clergy had crowded into the city; Augustine, seventy-five, watched churches burn across the province and took comfort in a wise man’s saying: ‘He is not to be thought great who thinks it strange that wood and stones should fall and mortals die.’ In the third month of the siege he fell ill with fever. He asked that ‘the shortest penitential Psalms of David’ be copied out and fixed to the wall opposite his bed, and he lay reading them and weeping. He asked that no one come in except the physicians and those bringing food, so that he could pray. He had always said, Possidius notes, that even a good Christian and bishop should not leave this life without repentance. He died on 28 August. He made no will, Possidius adds, ‘because as a poor man of God he had nothing from which to make it’ — the library he asked to be kept for the church. The city fell the following year. It is the last documented scene of the most documented pastor of antiquity, and it is a scene of penitence rather than triumph.
documentedStories.caveat: Possidius was an eyewitness and friend writing a memorial; the account is sober by the standards of the genre but is an admirer’s. The exact psalms are not specified beyond ‘the shortest penitential Psalms of David’.

uncertain: Cyprian's withdrawal in 250. His own letters give his reason: the crowd kept shouting for him, and he left for his people's peace, so as not to stir the riot further, and led them by letter. The Roman clergy's letter on the hired man who leaves the sheep, and his deacon Pontius's long defense, show that the withdrawal was questioned.

The charge behind the split at Carthage. The rival side said that the bishop who had made Caecilian bishop had handed over the Scriptures to be burned. Optatus, a Catholic bishop writing some sixty years later, says the charge was false, and quotes a hearing that cleared that bishop, Felix. The old sources give the split no year beyond soon after the great persecution.

The rival church speaks only through its enemies. Its own rule, that one who was stained could not wash away sins, survives in Optatus's quotation of its bishop Parmenian. Possidius says that in Augustine's early years the rebaptizing Donatist party held a large multitude of the Africans, while the Catholic church had long lain prostrate.

Who the heretics were at the Gladness. Augustine's letter says only that the sound of feasting came from the church of the heretics. That they were the Donatists rests on Possidius, who says Donatists lived in Hippo and the towns nearby. Optatus used the word differently: he called the Donatists schismatics, who had gone outside the church yet shared its true sacraments, and kept heretics for those who taught falsely about God.
The plague. Its account rests on Pontius, Cyprian's deacon and admirer, who says that people fled the sick and left their own, and that the dead lay through the whole city.

Several dates rest on modern reckoning, not on the old sources: Cyprian's election as bishop, the year of the plague, the years Augustine was made priest and bishop, and the years of his letters on the Gladness and on staying with the people.

sources.work: Cyprian, Letters, Latin text (ed. W. Hartel, CSEL 3.2, 1871), Letters 5, 14, 19, 20, 44, 55, 62 and 74
sources.note: Letter 5, from hiding in 250: nothing is to be lacking for the expenses of the confessors, those who had stood trial for the faith and been put in prison, or of the poor who stood firm; the priests who offered the Eucharist with the confessors in prison were to take turns, each with one deacon, so that the change of faces would stir less ill-will. Letter 14: the brief's Cyprian on deciding nothing alone. Letter 19: until peace returned, the bishops, meeting with the clergy and with the people who had stood firm, would settle everything by common counsel. Letter 20: his reason for withdrawing, so as not to stir the riot further. Letter 44: Novatian's envoys, kept from communion; later they burst into the gathering with shouting and demanded that their charges against the bishop of Rome already chosen be heard before the bishops and the people, and the bishops would not let a colleague chosen and approved by many be picked over by his rivals' abuse; they went on from house to house and town to town. Letter 55: no one is to be barred from penance and the hope of peace; when the persecution eased, many bishops met and set a long penance, each case examined. Letter 62: when raiders carried off Christian men, women and consecrated virgins, Cyprian wrote that their captivity must be counted Carthage's own, and the clergy and people of Carthage sent a hundred thousand sesterces to buy them back, with the names of all who gave. Letter 74: Stephen, bishop of Rome, as Cyprian quotes him, held that those who came from any heresy should have hands laid on them for repentance, and nothing new done; Cyprian held that washing outside the church was no baptism.

sources.note: The Acta are a court-style record of Cyprian's hearings joined to a Christian account of his death. The emperors Valerian and Gallienus ordered all who did not keep the Roman religion to take part in the Roman rites; Cyprian was first sent into exile at Curubis; at his arrest he was held at an officer's house, and when all his people gathered in the street before the door, he ordered that the girls be guarded; he was led out to a field, had twenty-five gold pieces given to the executioner, and the brethren laid cloths and napkins before him; he died on 14 September.

sources.work: Possidius, Life of Augustine, Latin and English (ed. and tr. H. T. Weiskotten, 1919)
sources.note: Possidius, bishop of Calama, was Augustine's friend for almost forty years and shared the siege of Hippo. The old bishop Valerius asked the people to provide a priest for the city; the Catholics laid hold of Augustine, standing among them, and brought him to be ordained while he wept, foreseeing, as he later told them, the dangers of governing a church. He preached in private and in public, at home and in the church, and listeners, the rival party's among them, brought shorthand writers to take down what he said; Donatists lived in Hippo and the nearby towns. Christians, and men of any sect, brought him their disputes, sometimes keeping him until mealtime, sometimes fasting all day; letters he wrote in people's worldly cases he counted a kind of forced service. When the church's money ran out he told the people he had nothing left for the poor, and for captives and the needy had the sacred vessels broken, melted and given out, though some judged it wrong. The Vandals, with Alans and Goths, crossed by sea from Spain and overran Africa; of countless churches only Carthage, Hippo and Cirta still stood. The siege lasted almost fourteen months, and in its third month Augustine fell ill; he preached in the church up to his last illness. Possidius copies Augustine's Letter 228 into the Life whole: one who is sought in particular may flee from city to city, so long as the others do not abandon the church; but when the danger is common to bishops, clergy and people, those who need others must not be abandoned by those they need; at such times people of both sexes and every age crowd into the church, some asking for baptism, some for reconciliation, some for penance.

sources.work: Augustine, Letters 29 and 93, Latin text (ed. A. Goldbacher, CSEL 34, 1895)
sources.note: Letter 29, written as priest of Hippo to Alypius, on the feast day of Leontius, a former bishop of Hippo. The people would not give up the feast they called the Gladness. Serving under the old bishop, Augustine read them Scripture against drunken feasts and pleaded with them until they wept together. Next day some still asked why now, when those before them had not forbidden it. He explained that after the persecutions, crowds of pagans used to feasting at their idols' festivals had been allowed feasts for the martyrs instead, for a time. On the feast day a greater crowd came, and men and women stayed singing psalms and hymns in the church until the light failed. Letter 93 in Latin: see the English below.

sources.work: Augustine, Letter 228, to Honoratus, Latin text (ed. A. Goldbacher, CSEL 57, 1911)

sources.work: Augustine, Letters 29 and 93 (tr. J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, 1, 1886)
sources.note: English of Letter 29. Letter 93, to a bishop of the rival church: at first Augustine held that no one should be forced into unity, only argued with; his colleagues pointed to his own town, brought over by fear of the emperors' laws, and he gave way; the laws punished the rival church with exile and fines, and the emperor Constantine first decreed that the property of those convicted of schism be confiscated. In the same letter, death is the penalty in the laws against heathen sacrifice, not against the rival church.

sources.note: Cyprian's feast was kept through all Africa, by Christians, pagans, Jews and heretics alike. Where a savage crowd had once gathered to shed his blood, a crowd now gathered to honor him, at an altar called Cyprian's table because he was offered there. The scan is damaged; the second half of the altar passage is confirmed by the Latin quoted in a note to Optatus's English.

sources.work: Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists (tr. O. R. Vassall-Phillips, 1917)
sources.note: Optatus, a Catholic bishop, wrote sixty years and more after the persecution. After it, Caecilian was chosen bishop of Carthage by the vote of the whole people; his opponents said the bishop who consecrated him had handed over the Scriptures, a charge Optatus calls false; they made Majorinus a rival bishop, and altar was raised against altar. He quotes the rival bishop Parmenian's rule that one who was stained could not wash away sins. He calls the Donatists schismatics who share true sacraments with the Catholics, and keeps heretics for those who falsified the creed. The persecution's order was that the Scriptures be burned, and he counts handing them over as betrayal, one of the two worst evils done in Africa; he quotes the hearing that cleared the consecrator, Felix.

quotationOriginals.modern: I did not move their tears with my own. But as these things were said, I confess, their weeping came first, and I could not hold back mine. When we had wept together, my sermon ended in the fullest hope that they would mend their ways.
quotationOriginals.printed: non ego illorum lacrimas meis lacrimis moui, sed cum talia dicerentur, fateor, eorum fletu praeuentus meum abstinere non potui, et cum iam pariter fleuissemus, plenissima spe correctionis illorum finis sermonis mei factus est.
quotationOriginals.work: Augustine, Letter 29.7, to Alypius (ed. A. Goldbacher, CSEL 34, 1895)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The scan prints a stray mark, a misread line number, before plenissima; it is left out here.
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: I did not move them to weep by first weeping myself; but while these things were being spoken, I own that, moved by the tears which they began to shed, I myself could not refrain from following their example. And when we had thus wept together, I concluded my sermon with full persuasion that they would be restrained by it from the abuses denounced.

quotationOriginals.modern: I could not write back alone. From my first days as bishop I resolved to do nothing on my own private judgment, without your counsel and the people's consent.
quotationOriginals.printed: solus rescribere nihil potui, quando a primordio episcopatus mei statuerim nihil sine consilio uestro et sine consensu plebis mea priuatim sententia gerere.

quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: I have not been able to reply by myself, since, from the first commencement of my episcopacy, I made up my mind to do nothing on my own private opinion, without your advice and without the consent of the people.

quotationOriginals.modern: But if the clergy are there, everyone is helped, as far as the Lord gives them strength. Some are baptized, others are reconciled. No one is cheated of communion in the Lord's body. All are comforted, built up and urged to ask God, who has the power to turn away all that is feared.
